div.p: Domitian was born on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, while his father was consul designate and due to enter on office in the following month, in the street of the sixth region of Rome known as "Pomegranate," in a house which afterwards he converted into a temple of the Flavian family. He is said to have passed his riper boyhood and early youth in such indigence and infamy, that he had not a single silver vessel in use; and it is an admitted fact that Clodius Pollio, a man of praetorian rank, against whom there is a poem of Nero's entitled "The One-eyed Man," had kept and on occasion produced a letter in Domitian's writing promising him an assignation; and there have not been wanting people to assert that Domitian was also debauched by Nerva, his immediate successor.

During the war against Vitellius he sought refuge in the Capitol with his uncle Sabinus and a part of the troops that were with him; but when the enemy were bursting in and the temple was in flames, he hid during the night in the sacristan's lodge, and in the morning, disguising himself in the garb of a worshipper of Isis and mingling with the priestlings of that variable superstition, he betook himself across the Tiber with one companion to the mother of a schoolmate of his, and lay so close that he could not be found by the searchers who had followed in his tracks.

It was not till after the victory of his party that he came forth from his retreat, and after being hailed as Caesar he took upon him the office of city praetor with consular power, but merely in name, for he handed over the administration of justice to his nearest colleague; in other respects, however, he exercised the full powers of an absolute ruler so lawlessly, that even then he showed what manner of man he would prove himself to be. Not to go into each detail, after taking liberties with the wives of many, he carried off Domitia Longina, the wife of Aelius Lamia, and actually married her; and in a single day he gave away over twenty offices in the city and the provinces, so that Vespasian kept saying that he wondered his son did not send a successor to him as well.

He also started on an expedition against Gaul and the Germanies quite unnecessarily and contrary to the advice of his father's friends, merely in order to put himself on an equality with his brother in power and rank. He was reprimanded for this, and to make him realize more fully his youth and position, he had to live with his father, and whenever they appeared in public, he followed in a litter the chair of his father and that of his brother, and mounted on a white horse he attended their joint triumph over Judaea. Furthermore, of his six consulships he held only one as an ordinary consul, and even that he owed to his brother's withdrawal and support.

He himself also made a wonderful pretence of modesty, and especially of an interest in poetry, an interest foreign to him previously and thrown aside with contempt later on, and he even gave readings publicly. Nevertheless, when Vologaesus, king of the Parthians, asked for auxiliaries against the Alani and for one of Vespasian's sons as commander, he strove might and main to be the one sent; and when the project fell through, he tried by gifts and promises to tempt other eastern kings to make the same request. And

On his father's death he hesitated for some time whether he should not offer the soldiers a double largess, and he had no qualms about asserting openly that he had been left a partner in the principate, but that the will had been falsified. from that time on he never ceased hatching plots against his brother secretly and openly, until finally, when Titus was seized by a grievous illness, before he had breathed his last, he ordered him to be abandoned as though already dead; and after his death he conferred no honour on him save that of deification, and he continued to attack him repeatedly by innuendo in his speeches and edicts.

In the early part of his reign he used to seek seclusion for some hours each day, doing nothing else but catching flies and stabbing them with a finely pointed writing-style. And so, when some one asked was there anybody inside with Caesar, Vibius Crispus wittily replied: "Not even a fly." Then he saluted as Augusta his wife Domitia, by whom he had had a son in his second consulship and < a daughter > in the following year; but he put her away by reason of her mad passion for the actor Paris, though he could not bear the separation from her, and took her back within a short time, pretending that the people so demanded.

In the administration of the empire he for some time showed himself variable, an equal blend of vices and virtues, until at last he let his virtues also be warped into vices. So far as one may surmise, it was contrary to his natural disposition that need made him grasping and fear made him cruel.

He constantly gave splendid and costly shows, not only in the amphitheatre but also in the Circus, where, besides the ordinary races for two-horsed and four-horsed chariots, he likewise presented two engagements in which cavalry and infantry separately joined battle; and in the amphitheatre he actually produced a naval fight. He even held wild-beast fights and gladiatorial conflicts at night-time by the light of lamps, and combats not merely between men but between women as well. He marked his unfailing attendance at the quaestors' games (which after a long discontinuance had been revived by him) by giving the people the privilege of calling for two pairs of gladiators from his own school, and had these brought in last of all accoutred in a manner worthy of the court.

Throughout each gladiatorial show there stood before his feet a little boy, dressed in scarlet, with a small and unnatural head, with whom he used to converse very freely, and sometimes seriously. At least, he was overheard to ask him if he knew why it had pleased him to make Mettius Rufus governor of Egypt at the last appointments to office. He also gave sea-fights in which fleets of almost full size took part, having hollowed out and encircled with seats a basin near the Tiber for the purpose; and he remained watching them to the very end amid a deluge of rain.

Moreover he celebrated the Secular games, calculating the period not from the year when Claudius had last given them, but from the year when Augustus had given them long before. During these games, in order to get through a hundred races more easily on the day of the Circus-sports, he shortened each race from seven rounds to five.

He also established in honour of Capitoline Jupiter a fiveyearly contest of a threefold nature, in music, horse-racing, and gymnastics, and considerably more crowns were given than nowadays. For there were competitions also in prose declamation in both Greek and Latin, and besides those who sang to their own lyre there were prizes for lyre-players accompanying a chorus and for those not accompanying a song; while in the stadium even girls competed in running. At these contests he himself presided in high Greek shoes, robed in a purple toga after the Greek fashion, and wearing on his head a golden crown
with the likenesses of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, while the priest of Jupiter and the college of the Flaviales sat beside him in similar attire, except that on their crowns was his likeness as well. He also celebrated at his Alban villa every year the Fiveday festival in honour of Minerva, for whom he had founded a college of priests, from which were drawn by lot those who should act as directors and provide splendid wild-beast fights and stage-plays, with contests in oratory and poetry besides.

On three occasions he gave to the people a largess of three hundred sesterces apiece, and during the gladiatorial spectacles at the festival of the Seven Hills he gave a very lavish banquet, distributing large food-baskets to the senate and knights, and small baskets to the common folk; and he himself was the first to begin to eat. On the following day he scattered a shower of presents of every kind, and because the greater portion happened to fall among the seats of the commons, he announced that fifty gift-tickets would be scattered over each block of the seats set apart for the equestrian and senatorial orders.

He restored a great many very stately buildings which had been consumed by fire, among them the Capitol, which had once more been burned; but all were inscribed with his name only, no mention being made of the original founders. He constructed a new temple on the Capitoline hill in honour of Jupiter Custos; likewise the Forum which nowadays bears the name of Nerva; also a temple to the Flavian family, a stadium, a concert-hall, and a basin for sea-fights, the stones of which served afterwards to rebuild the Circus Maximus, when its two sides had been destroyed by fire.

Of his military expeditions some he undertook voluntarily, others of necessity. Voluntarily that against the Chatti, of necessity one against the Sarmatians, after a legion and its commander had been cut to pieces, and two against the Dacians: the first upon the defeat of the consular Oppius Sabinus, the second upon the defeat of Cornelius Fuscus, prefect of the praetorian cohorts, to whom he had entrusted the whole conduct of the war. Over the Chatti and the Dacians, after sundry battles with varying success, he twice celebrated triumphs; for his victory over the Sarmatians he merely made offering of a laurel wreath to Jupiter on the Capitol.

The civil war, which Lucius Antonius, governor of Upper Germany, had stirred up, he brought to an end without being
personally present and by a wondrous piece of luck, for at the very hour of the engagement the sudden thawing of the Rhine prevented the barbarian forces from crossing to join Antonius. This victory he learned from portents before the news arrived, for on the same day as the decisive battle was fought a majestic eagle enveloped the statue of the emperor with its wings, uttering triumphant screams the while; and shortly afterwards reports of Antonius' death were so rife, that many maintained that they had actually seen his head brought into the city.

He also made many innovations in ordinary usages. He did away with the distribution of money doles to the people, and revived the custom of formal dinners. To the four parties of chariot-drivers in the Circus he added two with gold and purple as their liveries. He forbade actors appearing in the theatre, but allowed them the right of practising their art in private houses. He prohibited the castration of males, and put a limit on the price of the eunuchs whom the slavedealers still had in stock.

On one occasion when there was an extreme abundance of wine with an extreme scarcity of corn, thinking that the cornfields were being neglected by too great attention to the vineyards, he issued an edict forbidding the planting of new vines in Italy and ordering the cutting down of the vineyards in the provinces, not more than half, at most, of the existing vines to be left; but he did not persist in carrying out this reform. Some of the highest offices he opened equally to freedmen and Roman knights.

He prohibited the joining of the camps of separate legions and the depositing of more than a thousand sesterces by any one soldier in the camp-treasury, because it was manifest that Lucius Antonius, who had two legions in the one winter-quarters, had been encouraged to attempt a revolution partly by the amount of money thus deposited. He increased the soldiers' pay by three gold pieces, equivalent to a fourth annual payment.

He administered justice in a careful and energetic fashion, frequently holding special sittings on the tribunal in the Forum. He quashed such verdicts of the Hundred Judges as were given from interested motives. He repeatedly admonished the investigators of status to give no countenance to unsubstantial claims for freedom. He branded with infamy judges who accepted bribes, and their assessors as well.

He also directed the tribunes of the people to accuse of extortion an avaricious aedile and to get the senate to appoint commissioners to deal with his case. Moreover he exercised such diligence in keeping a check on the city magistrates and provincial governors, that at no period were they more cleanhanded and just; whereas after his time we have seen a great number of them charged with crimes of every kind.

When he took upon him the censorship of morals, he put an end to the licence prevalent in the theatres of the indiscriminate occupation of seats reserved for knights. Scandalous lampoons, published broadcast to defame men and women of position, he caused to be destroyed, and he degraded their authors. A man of quaestorian rank was expelled by him from the senate on account of his fondness for mimic gesturing and dancing. From women of loose morals he took away the use of the litter and the right of receiving legacies and inheritances. He struck off the jurors' list a Roman knight for taking back into wedlock a wife whom he had first divorced and then prosecuted for adultery. He condemned some men of both orders under the provisions of the Scantinian law. Incest on the part of the Vestal Virgins, which had been ignored even by his father and brother, he punished in diverse and merciless ways, earlier offences by capital punishment, and later offences in the ancient fashion.

For while he allowed the two sisters Oculata and also Varronilla a free choice of the manner of their death and banished their seducers, he later ordered Cornelia, a chief-priestess of the Vestals, who earlier had been acquitted but after a long interval retried and convicted, to be buried alive, and her paramours to be beaten to death with rods in the Comitium, with the exception of one of praetorian rank, who, when the case was by no means clear even at the rehearing, and the examination by torture had yielded no definite result, admitted his own guilt and was graciously allowed to go into exile.

To prevent anything sacred to the gods from being polluted with impunity, when a freedman of his had built a tomb for his son out of the stones set apart for the temple of Capitoline Jupiter, he caused it to be overthrown by his soldiers and the bones and ashes contained in it thrown into the sea.

At the beginning he had such an abhorrence of bloodshed in any form, that on one occasion, while his father was still absent from the city, happening to recall the line of Virgil : "Ere ever the impious race slew beeves to make them a banquet" he proposed to issue an edict that no oxen should be sacrificed. Also he gave hardly any grounds for being suspected of greed or parsimony either in a private capacity or for a long period of his reign; on the contrary, he frequently gave striking proofs not only of avoidance of gain, but even of liberality.

He treated his immediate circle in the most handsome fashion, and his primary and most urgent admonition to them was to shun all meanness. He refused to accept inheritances left to him by those who had children. He declared null and void a legacy in the will of Rustius Caepio, who had provided that his heir should distribute yearly a fixed sum of money to each separate senator on his first entry to the senate-house. All persons liable to prosecution, whose names had been posted in the public treasury for longer than the five years immediately preceding, he freed from the danger of trials, and would not allow charges against them to be renewed unless within a year and only on condition that an accuser who did not make good his case should be punished with exile.

To quaestors' clerks, who, in accordance with custom, though contrary to the Clodian law, had been engaged in trading, he granted pardon for what was past. Strips of land which here and there remained over when allotments were made to the veterans he granted to the old occupiers as theirs by a prescriptive right. False charges which enriched his private treasury he curbed by heavy penalties on the accusers, and this saying of his was current : "An emperor who does not punish informers rouses their activities."

But he did not continue in this course of clemency or self-denial, though he lapsed somewhat sooner into cruelty than into avarice. He put to death a pupil of the pantomimist Paris, while he was still of immature years and sick at the time, merely because in talent and figure he seemed not unlike his master; also Hermogenes of Tarsus because of some veiled allusions in his History, and he crucified the very scribes who had copied it. Because the head of a household said that a Thracian gladiator was a match for his opponent, but no match for the giver of the show, he had him dragged from his seat into the arena and thrown to the dogs with this label upon him: "A partizan of the Thracians who spoke blasphemously."

He executed many senators, of whom a number had been consuls; among them Civica Cerealis, even when proconsul of Asia, Salvidienus Orfitus and Acilius Glabrio, then in exile, on the pretext that they were plotting revolution; the rest on the most flimsy charges: Aelius Lamia on account of some pleasantries, undoubtedly such as to excite suspicion but uttered a long time before and quite harmless, because he, after his wife had been taken away from him, had said to someone who praised his voice: "Continence keeps me in training," and because he had replied to Titus who was urging him to a second marriage: "Surely you too are not going to take a wife?";

Salvius Cocceianus, for having celebrated the birthday of his own uncle, the emperor Otho; Mettius Pompusianus, because it was commonly reported that he had a horoscope predicting empire and carried about with him a map of the world on parchment and the speeches of kings and generals from Titus Livius, besides having given to slaves of his the names of Mago and Hannibal; Sallustius Lucullus, military governor of Britain, for allowing lances of a new shape to be called “Lucullean'; Junius Rusticus, because he had published panegyrics of Paetus Thrasea and Helvidius Priscus and styled them the most saintly of men, an offence which gave occasion to the edict banishing all philosophers from the city and from Italy.

He likewise executed Helvidius the son, the reason assigned being that in a theatrical after-piece he had, under the characters of Paris and Oenone, censured the emperor's divorce from his wife; also Flavius Sabinus, one of his own two cousins, because on the day of the consular elections when he was to be designated for the consulship, the herald by inadvertence proclaimed him to the people not as "consul" but as "Imperator."

But after his victory in the civil war he became much more cruel, and he subjected many of the opposite party, in order to discover their confederates who still lurked hidden, to a new form of examination by torture, putting fire to their private parts; in the case of some he also cut off their hands. Moreover it is an undoubted fact that of the better-known only two were granted pardon, a tribune of senatorial rank and a centurion, who, to establish more readily their freedom from guilt, proved that they were men of vile unchastity and, as such, could not have had any influence with the commander or with the troops.

His cruelty was not only intense, but also subtle and unexpected. The very day before he put his accountant upon the cross he called him into his own chamber, made him sit down on the couch beside him, and sent him away a carefree and a cheerful man; he even deigned to give him a portion from his table. At the time when he was about to condemn to death the ex-consul Arrecinus Clemens, one of his confidants and spies, he treated him with the same, or even greater, favour, till finally, when he was riding with him in a litter, he caught sight of his denouncer and said: "Is it your pleasure that to-morrow we should give audience to this good-for-nothing slave?"”

And to abuse the patience of men still more contemptuously, he never pronounced an unusually harsh sentence without some prefatory remarks in a merciful strain, so that there came to be no surer sign of a savage conclusion than the mildness of his opening words. On one occasion he brought into the senate-house certain persons charged with high treason, and when he began by declaring that he would test that day his dearness to the senate, he had no difficulty in getting them condemned to the death-penalty inflicted in the old-fashioned way;

then, alarmed at the frightfulness of this punishment, in order to lessen the odium, he vetoed it in these words (for it will be instructive to learn them precisely): "Allow me, Conscript Fathers, to obtain from your devotion a favour which I know I shall find difficulty in obtaining, that you will graciously grant to the condemned a free choice of the manner of their death; for thus you will spare your own eyes, and all the world will understand that I was at the meeting of the senate."

Impoverished by his outlay on buildings and spectacles, as well as by the addition which he had made to the military pay, he tried the expedient of reducing the number of soldiers, to lighten the expense of the standing armies. But when he found that this left him open to the attacks of the barbarians, without extricating him from the embarrassment of his financial burdens, he had no hesitation in practising every kind of plunder. The goods of the living and the dead were everywhere seized, it mattered not who was the accuser or what the charge. It sufficed to allege an action or utterance of any sort prejudicial to the majesty of the emperor.

Estates of utter strangers were confiscated, provided any one person came forward to say that he had heard from the deceased, while still alive, that Caesar was his heir. The impost which constituted the "Jewish revenue" was enforced more rigorously than all the rest. Evasion of this was made a charge against those who were living in the Jewish fashion without being registered as such, and those who concealed their nationality and did not pay the tribute imposed on their people. I myself remember being present in my youth when an old man of ninety was examined before a procurator and a crowded bench to see if he were circumcised.

From his youth up there was nothing of the fellow-citizen in his disposition; on the contrary, he was presumptuous and extravagant both in words and deeds. When Caenis, his father's concubine, on her return from Histria offered to kiss him, as she always did, he extended his hand for her to kiss. Indignant that his brother's son-in-law should also have servants liveried in white, he exclaimed : "It is not good that there be many chiefs."

When he became emperor, he did not scruple to boast in the senate that he had given the imperial power to both his father and his brother, and that they had but restored to him what was his own; nor, on taking back his wife after their separation, to proclaim that she was recalled to his divine couch. He delighted to hear the people in the amphitheatre on the feast day shouting: "Luck to our Master and Mistress!" And what is more, when at the Capitoline contest the whole audience with one voice implored him to restore Palfurius Sura, who had been banished some time before from the senate and now had won the crown for oratory, he deigned no reply, but merely by the voice of a herald bade them be silent.

With like arrogance, when he was dictating a draft of an official letter in the name of his procurators, he began thus: "Our Master and our God ordains that this be done." After this it became the established custom that none should address him by any other title either in writing or in speech. He allowed no statues to be set up to him on the Capitol, unless of gold and silver and of a certain weight. Throughout the different quarters of the city he erected so many and such huge covered passage-ways and arches adorned with four-horsed chariots and triumphal tokens, that on one of them somebody inscribed in Greek: "It is enough!"

took seventeen consulships in all, a greater number than any of his predecessors; the seven in the middle he held in sequence, but all of them in an almost nominal sense, none of them beyond the Kalends of May, and many of them only till the Ides of January. Furthermore, after two triumphs, and as he had taken He to himself the surname "Germanicus," he changed the names of the months September and October, calling them in accordance with his own titles "Germanicus" and "Domitianus," because in the former month he had entered upon his empire and he was born in the latter.

By such conduct he made himself dreaded and hated by all, and at last he was crushed by a conspiracy of his friends and favourite freedmen, to which his wife was also privy. For a long time past he had had a premonition of the last year and day of his life, and even of the very hour and nature of his death. While he was still a mere stripling, the Chaldaeans had foretold it all; his father, too, had once openly made sport of him at table for refusing mushrooms and thus showing ignorance of his fate in not rather fearing steel.

Consequently he was always apprehensive and nervous, and was upset beyond measure by even the slightest suspicions. In allowing his published edict about the cutting down of vines to become void he is commonly believed to have been influenced by nothing more strongly than by the scattering of leaflets containing these lines: "Gnaw to my roots, if thou wilt, O goat, my fruit shall be yielding Wine quite enough to pour, when as a victim thou'rt slain."

It was this same dread which led him, though he was most covetous of such distinctions, to refuse a new and cunningly devised honour offered by the senate, who had decreed that whenever he held the consulship Roman knights chosen by lot wearing the purple-striped toga and bearing military lances should walk before him among the lictors and attendants.

But as the time of the suspected danger drew nigh, he became more anxious every day, and he had the walls of the colonnades, in which he took his walks, studded with phengite stone, so that he might see in its brilliant surface a reflection of what was taking place behind him. He gave a hearing to prisoners in most cases only in private and alone, even holding their chains in his hands. Also, by way of convincing his household that the death of the master was a thing not to be ventured on even from exemplary motives, he condemned to execution Epaphroditus, his secretary for petitions, because he was believed to have lent a helping hand to the deserted Nero in taking his own life.

Lastly, there was Flavius Clemens, his own cousin, a man of most despicable sloth, whose sons, when yet of tender age, he had openly designated to succeed him, and abolishing their former names had ordered the one to be called "Vespasian" and the other "Domitian,'' him of a sudden, when his consulship had barely expired, Domitian put to death on the most shadowy suspicion. It was this deed which above all else hastened his own destruction.

For eight months in succession so many lightning-strokes occurred and were reported, that he exclaimed: "Let him now strike whom he will." The Capitol was struck and the temple of the Flavian family; also the palace on the Palatine and his own bedchamber. Furthermore, an inscription-plate on the base of his triumphal statue was torn off by a violent gale and fell on a neighbouring tomb. The tree which had been overturned and had risen anew, while Vespasian was still a private citizen, then suddenly fell down once more. The goddess Fortune at Praeneste, who throughout his whole reign when he invoked her blessing on the new year had been wont to give him an oracle of happy import and always the same, now in his last year sent him a most gloomy one, in which there was mention of bloodshed.

He dreamt that Minerva, whom he worshipped with a superstitious reverence, departed from her shrine declaring that she could no longer protect him, since she had been disarmed by Jupiter. Nothing, however, disquieted him so much as the answer given by the astrologer Ascletarion and what befell him. When he was accused by informers and made no denial that he had talked openly of what his art enabled him to foresee, Domitian asked him if he knew what end awaited himself. He confidently replied that he would shortly be torn by dogs; whereupon Domitian commanded that he should be put to death at once, but also, in order to expose the vain pretensions of his art, that he should be given most careful funeral. When this was being done, it happened that a sudden storm scattered the pyre, and dogs tore the half-burnt corpse, and that this was recounted to the emperor at dinner among the other gossip of the day by the actor Latinus, who had chanced to notice it as he passed by.

On the day before he was killed, when he had ordered some apples which were served to him to be kept till the morrow,
he added: "If only I am spared to enjoy them!''; and turning to those close to him he declared that on the following day the moon in Aquarius would imbrue herself with blood, and that a deed would be done of which men would speak the whole world over. About midnight he became so terrified that he sprang from his couch. Then in the morning he heard the case of a soothsayer sent to him from Germany, who when consulted about a lightning-stroke had foretold a change of rulers, and he sentenced him to death.

While scratching overhardly a festered wart upon his forehead he made the blood flow, and exclaimed: "May it stop at this!" He asked what hour it was, whereupon, instead of the fifth hour of which he stood in dread, the sixth was purposely announced to him. Cheered by this, and as though the danger were already past, he was hastening to refresh his body, when Parthenius, the chief chamberlain, turned him from his purpose by announcing that a bearer of some weighty tidings had come and should not be put off. Accordingly he dismissed all others and withdrew into his bedchamber, where he was slain.

With regard to the nature of the plot and the manner of his death the facts which became public were mainly these. As the conspirators were undecided when and how, that is to say, whether to attack him in the bath or at dinner, Stephanus, the steward of Domitilla, who at that time was under the charge of misappropriating money, offered his advice and aid. To avert suspicion, he kept his left arm enveloped in wool and bandages for some days, as though it were injured, and when the hour was at hand he inserted a stiletto in the wrapping. Then alleging that he had a conspiracy to disclose and gaining admission on this account, while the emperor was reading the proffered document and was dumbfounded by the contents, he stabbed him in the groin.

When, in spite of his wound, he made resistance, Clodianus, a miltary adjutant, and Maximus, a freedman of Parthenius, and Satur, an upper chamberlain, and an unnamed person from the gladiatorial school all fell upon him and butchered him with seven wounds. A page, while waiting, as his manner was, beside the altar of the Lares in the bed-chamber, was present at the murder and recounted this further fact, that he was ordered by Domitian, immediately he had received the first wound, to hand him the dagger concealed beneath his pillow and to call the serving-men, but that he found nothing at the head of the couch except the hilt, and moreover found every outlet barred. In the meanwhile the emperor had grappled with Stephanus, dragged him to the ground, and struggled with him for long, at one moment striving to wrest from him the stiletto, at another to gouge out his eyes, notwithstanding his torn fingers.

He was killed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in his forty-fifth year and the fifteenth year of his reign. His body was carried out on a common bier by a pauper's bearers, and his nurse Phyllis burned it at her suburban villa on the Latin Way; but his relics she brought by stealth into the temple of the Flavian family and mingled them with the ashes of Titus' daughter Julia, whom she had also reared.

He was tall of stature, with a modest and very ruddy countenance, and large eyes, though his vision was somewhat dim. Moreover he was shapely and graceful, especially during his youth, and indeed in his whole person, save only his feet, the toes of which were too drawn in. Later in life he was further disfigured by baldness, corpulence, and the slenderness of his legs, though it was through a long illness that they had become so thin.

He was so fully conscious that his modest looks were a recommendation, that he once made this boast in the senate: "Up till now, at any rate, you have approved my disposition and my countenance." Baldness annoyed him so much that he took it as a personal affront if another was twitted with it either by way of jest or taunt; and yet in a treatise "On the Care of the Hair," which he published and dedicated to a friend, he inserted as a consolation both to the other and himself these words: "Seest thou not that I too am comely and stately of figure? And yet the same fate for my hair awaits me, and I bear with fortitude the ageing of my locks in youth. Realize then that nothing is more charming than beauty, and nothing more fleeting."

Finding all exertion irksome, he rarely went through the city on foot. In the field and on the march he rode but seldom, and was constantly carried in a litter. He took no interest in exercises of arms, but a surpassing interest in archery. There are many who have seen him at his Alban retreat repeatedly despatch wild beasts of various kinds by the hundred, and purposely pierce the heads of some of them in such a way that with two arrow-hits he produced the semblance of a pair of horns. At times a slave would stand at a distance holding out as a tiny target the palm of his right hand with the fingers spread, and he aimed his arrows with such skill that they all passed harmlessly through the spaces between the fingers.

He neglected liberal studies when he became ruler, though he took care to restore at very great cost the libraries destroyed by fire, searching in every quarter for specimens of the lost works, and sending scribes to Alexandria to make fresh copies and to correct others. Yet he never applied himself to a knowledge of history or poetry, nor even to such writing as his duties demanded. Beyond the memoirs and transactions of Tiberius Caesar he had no favourite reading; in composing his letters, speeches, and edicts he employed another's brains. Yet there was no want of grace in his conversation, and at times his mots were quite noteworthy: "I would like," said he, "to be as handsome as Maecius thinks he is"; and of somebody's head, with hair both reddish and flecked with white, he said: "It is snow on which mead has been poured." "The lot of princes," he used to remark, is most pitiable, since no one will believe the plots they have detected, unless they have been murdered."

In his periods of leisure he used to amuse himself with dicing, even on working days and in the forenoon hours. He bathed early in the day and lunched to repletion, so that it was a rare thing for him to take more at dinner than a Matian apple and a small draught from a flagon. He gave frequent and lavish banquets, but went through them almost with a rush; in no case did he prolong them beyond sunset or follow them with a carouse; for until bedtime he did nothing but take a solitary walk in a secluded spot.

He was abnormally lustful, and his constant intercourse with women he styled "bed-wrestling," as though it were a form of exercise. Scandal had it that he made smooth his concubines with his own hand and swam with the commonest courtesans. His brother's daughter, who was offered to him in marriage while she was yet a maid, he most stubbornly refused to wed, as he was already fettered by his union with Domitia; shortly afterwards, when she was given in wedlock to another, he was ready enough to seduce her, and that too while Titus was still alive. Later, when she was bereft of father and of husband, he loved her with a most intense and undisguised passion, so that he even came to be the cause of her death by forcing her to abortion of an offspring of his.

The people bore his murder with indifference, but the soldiers took it sorely to heart and forthwith tried to give him the title of "Deified," while they were quite ready to avenge him, had they not lacked leaders. Shortly afterwards, however, they effected their purpose by demanding most insistently the surrender for punishment of the authors of his death. The senate, on the contrary, were so exultant that they vied in their haste to fill the senate-house, and did not refrain from tearing to pieces the dead emperor by outcries of a most insulting and virulent kind. They even ordered ladders to be brought in and his medallion-portraits and images to be torn down before their eyes and dashed there and then upon the ground; finally they decreed that his inscriptions everywhere should be erased, and all record of him wiped out for ever.

Some few months before his murder a crow on the Capitol uttered the words "All will be well," nor was there wanting some one to interpret the omen in this wise: "On the Tarpeian summit a crow which lately alighted Could not declare 'It is well,' only declared 'It will be.'" They say, too, that Domitian himself dreamt that a golden hump grew out behind his shoulders, and he was fully persuaded that this portended that after him the condition of the commonwealth would be more happy and more prosperous; and so it shortly proved to be through the integrity and mildness of the rulers who came after.
